PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #1: Recognize opinion topics — Grade 4

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that informative writing teaches facts and narrative writing shares stories. But there is a third kind of writing — persuasive writing — where the writer shares what he thinks or believes about a topic. Today, I'm going to teach you how to recognize if a writer/author is sharing an opinion — or not.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing starts with an opinion. An opinion tells what the writer thinks, feels, or believes about a topic that has different sides or choices. Unlike facts — which are right or wrong — opinions are neither. They are simply different. Two people can read about the same topic and believe completely different things. (Introduce the icons & hand gestures.)

When a reader recognizes that a piece of writing is persuasive, he understands: the writer is going to share what HE thinks and explain why his choice is best.

WHY the skill is important | If a reader cannot tell the difference between opinions and facts, he may confuse what the writer believes with fact. This gets trickier in fourth grade — because persuasive writing actually includes facts, details, and real examples. The writer uses those facts to support his opinion. That means a persuasive piece can sound a lot like an informative piece. When readers recognize persuasive writing, they understand: "This is what the author believes — and he is using facts to convince me." Then they can read and decide whether or not to agree.

HOW the skill works | After reading a little bit of the text…
1. ASK: Is the author describing what happened to characters? If yes, then it's a narrative story.
2. ASK: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? If yes — it's informative writing. But remember — persuasive writing also includes facts. So if you see facts, don't stop there. Keep questioning the author's purpose.
3. ASK: Is the author sharing his thoughts and feelings AND occasionally stating facts and details to support it? (The facts are there to support the opinion, not replace it.) Also look for subtle opinion words & adjectives — words like "should/not, most, best, important, better, necessary." Could someone have a different opinion on this same topic? If yes — it's persuasive writing.

This is how readers determine whether the writer's purpose is to describe a narrative story, inform with facts, or persuade the audience with his opinion.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I figure out what type of writing this is. Project P.E. Text A and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a main character. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to individual sentences.) "Stretching increases flexibility and reduces the risk of injury." That's a fact — everyone agrees on that. "Muscles that are warmed up can move more easily." True — that's how the body works. (Pause.) Everything here sounds like facts everyone agrees on. But persuasive includes facts, too. So I'm going to double check by asking another set of questions.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts & feelings & occasionally stating facts and details to support it? (Scan slowly, pointing to each sentence.) "Taking time to stretch is an important part of any physical activity." Important — could that be an opinion word? (Pause.) Let me think. Would everyone agree that stretching is important? Actually — yes. This is widely accepted. It's not really a debatable side. (Pause.) And I don't see the facts here working to convince me of a position. They are simply explaining how stretching works. (Shake head.) This is informative writing.

OK, I'm going to do this again. I'm going to determine the author's purpose for writing. Project P.E. Text B and quickly read it aloud to yourself. Do not ask students to comment.
1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? (Scan the text.) I don't see a character or a problem. Nothing is happening to anyone. This is NOT a narrative.
2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? (Point to the first sentence.) "Daily movement helps build strength and endurance." That sounds like a fact. "Physical activity supports better concentration in the classroom." That could be true. (Pause.) But just seeing facts doesn't mean this is automatically informative. I know persuasive writing uses facts, too. Let me think about this through the persuasive lens.
3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts & feelings & occasionally stating facts and details to support it? (Point to the first sentence.) "Having P.E. every day would improve student health and focus." Improve — opinion word. Would everyone agree? Some might argue daily P.E. takes too much time away from academics. (Point to the last sentence.) "Daily P.E. would benefit both learning and overall well-being." Benefit — another opinion word. Not everyone agrees on what benefits students most. (Pause.) Ahh, I'm noticing how the facts are working to convince me that daily P.E. is a good idea. It's persuasive!

Today, we are learning how to recognize the signals that indicate an author is sharing his opinion within persuasive writing.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example. Project Fire Drill Text A. Read it aloud quickly. Do not ask students to comment.

1. Ask: Is the author describing what happened to characters? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop for 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say no — there's no character and nothing is happening to anyone. Let's keep going.

2. Ask: Is the author teaching facts everyone agrees on? Point to "Repeated practice builds confidence and reduces confusion." and "Students learn exactly where to go and what to do." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say those sound like facts — and they do. But persuasive includes some facts. Let's keep asking.

3. Ask: Is the author sharing his thoughts & feelings supported by facts? Point to "Regular fire drills are an essential part of school safety." Is "essential" a fact or opinion word? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. Ooh… this is a tough one. "Could someone argue that other safety measures are MORE important?" (Nod.) What about "builds confidence," "reduces confusion," "prevent panic" — are those facts to teach us or convince us? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. Right — this is persuasive!

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to tell when a writer is sharing his opinion — or not. If we can recognize opinions, then we are closer to being able to write them.

During Independent Writing Time, your job is to read several short texts and apply the same process. You will mark the text with a "P" if you determine it's persuasive and shares an opinion. Mark an "I" if it's informative and teaches facts. Mark an "E" if it's an entertaining narrative story. Now it's your turn!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (1 of 2) — Grade 4

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
We know that persuasive writing isn't just about what you think — it's about what you can prove. But how do you know which side you can prove best before you start writing? Today, I'm going to teach you how to think through both sides of a topic to determine the strongest side.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing is more than just your opinion — it's the strongest opinion you can prove. Writers don't pick a side right away and start writing. Instead, they determine the strongest side by carefully thinking through both choices before committing to one. The strongest side isn't necessarily the one you like best — it's the one you can best prove.

WHY the skill is important | If a writer picks a side too quickly — based only on gut feeling — he may choose the harder side to prove. And "harder to prove" means exactly that: when he sits down to write, he can't think of what to say. Thinking through both sides first helps you find the one that you have the most to say about. And in persuasive writing, it's all about convincing the reader, and you need A LOT of details to make your point.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Look at the persuasive topic and identify both choices. Don't lean either direction yet — just name them side by side and treat them equally.

Step 2: Zip it. Before thinking begins, run your finger across your lips — zip them shut. (Demonstrate the zipper gesture.) Your opinion is locked inside. It's not gone — it's just waiting. You are not allowed to unzip until you have thought carefully through BOTH sides. This is how writers avoid rushing to a decision.

STEP 3: Think like one side. (Reveal the blue hat.) Writers put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best. Think like someone who genuinely loves this choice — even if you don't. (Teach students to use their hands and mime placing a hat on their heads.)

To generate strong details, try these strategies.
• Picture someone you know who would love this choice. What would they say is great about it?
• Think small — don't just say "it's fun" or "it's good." Ask yourself: what exactly happens? What does it look, feel, smell, taste, or sound like? Small specific details are always stronger than big general ones.
• Think about what you've seen or heard — a commercial, a conversation, something a friend or family member said. That counts as thinking.

When you've thought of everything you can for that side, take the hat off. (Introduce the gesture of picking up a hat, putting it on, thinking, taking it off, then switching to the other hat.)

STEP 4: Think like the other side. (Take off the blue hat and put on the red one.) Now think like someone who loves the OTHER choice — even if it's not your favorite. Use the same three strategies. Give this side the same honest effort you gave the first one. Your zipper stays shut until you've done both.

This is how writers determine the strongest side — by thinking through both before choosing.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I do this.

Step 1: Name both sides. My topic is: What is better — drive-thru or ordering and eating inside? (Display the choices within a T-Chart.) Those are my two choices. I'm not picking — just naming them.

Step 2: Zip it. My first thought is already in my head. (Run finger across lips — zip.) Locked. Not saying it yet. I have to think through both sides first.

Step 3: Think like one side. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I'm putting on the Drive-Thru thinking cap. Let me think like someone who really loves the drive-thru.

OK — think small. What actually happens at a drive-thru? You never even get out of the car. If it's raining or freezing outside — you don't care. You just roll down the window. Little kids stay buckled in their car seats — no unbuckling, no carrying, no chaos. And here's a detail I heard someone say once: you can go through the drive-thru in your pajamas and nobody knows. (Laugh to yourself.) What else? You grab your food and you're gone. No parking spot, no walking across a lot, no waiting for a table. If you're on a road trip, a drive-thru stop is fast — you barely lose any time. Once I started thinking small, the details just kept coming. (Take the hat off.) I'm done thinking like a drive-thru person.

Step 4: Think like the other side. (Hold up the red hat but don't put it on yet.) Now I have to think like someone who loves eating inside. Honestly, I'm usually in a hurry — drive-thru is fine with me. But I have to zip it and borrow someone else's brain. (Put on the red hat.)

Let me picture someone who loves sitting down inside a restaurant. They walk in, find a table, stretch their legs after a long car ride — that actually feels good after being cramped. They can see the menu up close and take their time choosing. They get free refills. Extra ketchup. Extra napkins — right there at the table.

Think small — what else actually happens? You can go wash your hands before you eat. You can get up and use the bathroom. You sit and talk and laugh with whomever you're with — you're not balancing food on your lap or trying to eat while someone's driving. (Pause.) And what have I heard people say? I've heard parents say eating inside feels like an actual meal — not just grabbing food and rushing off somewhere.

Today, we are learning how to push ourselves to think of small, specific details for both sides — even the side we don't know well or wouldn't normally choose.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another example.
1. Name both sides. The topic is: Which is the best treat — candy bar or ice cream?
2. Zip it. Locked. Think first.
3. Think like one side. (Blue hat on — students mime.) Candy Bar thinking cap. Don't just say "candy bars taste good." Think small! Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard the smell of chocolate when you unwrap it, the gooey caramel stretching when you take a bite, breaking off a piece to share, etc. (Hat off — students mime.)
4. Think like the other side. (Red hat on — students mime.) Now think like an ice cream lover — even if that's not your first choice. Think small. Picture someone standing at the counter choosing flavors. What exactly makes them love it? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6–10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard licking the cone before it melts, stacking two flavors, cold and creamy on your tongue, trying a new flavor every time. See how thinking small makes even the unexpected side feel full of details?

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic — pushing ourselves to think small and find specific details, even for the side we wouldn't naturally choose.

During Independent Writing Time, you and your partner will think through both sides of this topic: Which is the best vacation — winter break or summer break? When I project the topic, work with your partner to think of every small, specific detail you can for one side. Then switch hats and do the same for the other side. How many details can you two come up with? Now it's your turn!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #2: Determine the strongest side (2 of 2) — Grade 4

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Yesterday we learned how to think through both sides of a persuasive topic — putting on each thinking cap and pushing ourselves to think of small, specific details for both sides. Today I'm going to teach you how to jot down the details you think of for each side. This will bring us one step closer to determining the strongest side.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Yesterday you thought through both sides of a persuasive topic. But thinking alone isn't enough — ideas that stay in your head slip away before they ever make it into writing. Jotting captures each detail on paper during prewriting. Jotting means writing a concise phrase — 1-4 words to preserve the thinking without slowing down the process. (Connect to research unit jotting if previously taught — Skill 1, Day 2. Review shortcuts and abbreviations.)

WHY the skill is important | A persuasive writer's goal isn't just to list details — it's to jot as many details for BOTH sides as he can think of during prewriting. This is critical to determining the strongest side.

HOW the skill works |
Step 1: Name both sides. Write one choice at the top of each side of the T-Chart — blue hat side on the left, red hat side on the right. Both sides start equal.

Step 2: Zip it. (Zipper gesture — students mime.) Lock in your first instinct. Don't let it out yet. A writer who commits too early may miss the stronger argument entirely.

STEP 3: Think like one side & jot. (Reveal the blue hat. Students mime.) Put on the thinking cap of someone who believes this side is best. Jot each detail in 1–4 words, on its own line, & stacking it down that side. Writers typically begin with one side and continue until ideas slow.

If you fill every line on that side before you're finished thinking — grab a second T-Chart and continue on the same side. The other side stays empty for now. Stay in that thinking cap until every detail is captured. (Remove blue hat. Students mime.)

STEP 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Put on the red hat. Students mime.) Now think like someone who loves the OTHER choice. Jot each detail on its own line, stacking down that side. Give this side the same honest effort.

Writers typically begin with one side and continue until ideas slow down. However, sometimes while making the second list (Side B), the writer has a new thought for Side A. No problem. Jump over to Side A and jot it. Then return to Side B and continue listing details.

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I jot details for both sides of my persuasive topic.

Step 1: Name both sides. Yesterday my topic was: What is better — drive-thru or ordering and eating inside? (Display a blank T-Chart.) I write one choice at the top of each side. (Write Drive-thru on the left & Order/Eat In on the right.) There — both sides are named.

Step 2: Zip it. (Run finger across lips — zip.)

Step 3: Think like one side & jot. (Place the blue hat on your head.) I've got my Drive Thru thinking cap on. Yesterday I thought of several details for this side. Now I jot them — 1–4 words each, stacking down the left side.

(Jot while narrating details.)
• Never get out — car
• Rain/cold — don't care
• Kids stay buckled
• PJs — nobody knows
• Grab food & go
• No parking, no walking
• Road trip — barely lose time

Once I started jotting, the details stacked up fast. (Take the hat off.) I think I'm done thinking like a Drive Thru person.

Step 4: Think like the other side & jot. (Hold up the red hat — don't put it on yet.) Now I have to like someone who loves eating inside. I'm usually in a hurry — drive-thru is fine with me. But I have to zip it and borrow someone else's brain. (Put on the red hat.) Any details I come up with now, will all go on the right side — under "Order & Eat Inside." (Point at T-Chart.)

• I'm picturing someone walking in, finding a table, stretching their legs. (Jot: "stretch legs.")
• See menu up close — take time choosing. (Jot: "see menu, choose.")
• Free refills. (Jot: "free refills.")
• Wash hands before eating. (Jot: "wash hands.")
• Extra ketchup, extra napkins. (Jot: "extra ketchup/napkins.")

(Pause.) Wait — I just thought of something for the Drive-Thru side. (Switch hats.) When you do a lot of drive-thrus, you have a whole pile of extra napkins in the glove compartment. This is valuable! I have to jump back to Side A and capture that before I lose it. (Jot: "extra napkins.")

OK — back to eating inside. (Switch hats back.)
• Sit, talk & laugh with whoever you're with. (Jot: "sit, talk & laugh.")
• Feels like an actual meal — not rushing. (Jot: "actual meal, no rush.")

Today, we are learning how to jot details for both sides of a persuasive topic — capturing specific details on paper so we can eventually determine the strongest side.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Yesterday, you thought about which is the better treat — a candy bar or ice cream? Help me jot down those details. (Reveal a new T-Chart.)

1. Name both sides. Point in the air — where do I write down the two sides, the two choices? Yes, Candy bar by the blue hat & Ice cream by the red hat.

2. Zip it. Locked. Think first.

3. Think like one side & jot. (Blue hat on — students mime.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — "smell choc, melt in mouth, gooey & stretchy caramel, easy to share = break," etc.

4. Think like the other side & jot. (Switch hats.) Guide students to think, Turn & Talk, and help you jot one detail at a time — licking, stack scoops & flavors, creamy, try new flavors, cold on tongue, etc. Does any of this make you think of another detail about Candy bar? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard some of you say that chocolate is thick & creamy, too. (Switch hats & jot it.)

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
Writers, today we learned how to think & jot down details for BOTH sides of a persuasive. This is an important step before we can determine the strongest side.

During Independent Writing Time, you will fill out a T-Chart for which is the best vacation — winter break or summer break. This time you will work alone. (Yesterday you brainstormed with a partner. Today, you will jot down the details by yourself.) Think of all the details you can for one side before switching to the other side. And if you need a second T-Chart, I've got extra ones right here. Now it's your turn!

PERSUASIVE WRITING SKILL #3: Write an opinion — Grade 4

STEP 1 (Introduce — I do; you watch & listen):
Up until now, everything we have done in our persuasive unit has been prewriting — thinking through both sides and determining the strongest one. Today we transition from prewriting to drafting. The first thing a persuasive writer does in his draft is tell the audience which side he has chosen. Today, I'm going to teach you how to write a strong opinion statement at the beginning of any persuasive piece.

STEP 2A (Tell the children — 5 minutes):
WHAT the skill is | Persuasive writing begins with an opinion statement. The first sentence tells the audience exactly what the writer thinks and which side he has chosen. This is no longer prewriting — this is the moment the writer goes public with his thinking.

WHY the skill is important | Without a clear opinion statement at the opening, the reader has no anchor — he doesn't know what side the writer is on or what the writing is trying to prove. By stating the opinion first, the writer signals his position immediately and sets up everything that follows. Remember — the goal of persuasive writing is to convince the audience to agree. So get to the point fast.

HOW the skill works |
STEP 1. Name the strongest side. Look back at your T-Chart. Find the side circled — the one with the most details and proof. The word or words labeling that side belong in your opinion sentence.

STEP 2. Name the bigger topic. This is typically found in the writing prompt. It's the broader subject the two sides come from — usually 1–3 words. It gives the reader context so the opinion doesn't appear out of nowhere.

STEP 3. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. (Connect to SKILL #1 — opinion signal words.) By intermediate grades, writers rarely use "I think" or "I believe" in persuasive writing. Opinion language is much more subtle. It's drops a single word — like "should, clearly, or best" — rather than a sentence starter. Test out 3 different opinion words as options for the first sentence.

STEP 4. Put the 3 parts together. Combine all 3 items in one oral sentence: strongest side + bigger topic + opinion word. Try it different ways, each time using different opinion language. Listen for the version that is most direct, most confident, and most specific. The stronger and more precise that opening statement, the more confident and convincing the entire piece feels from the first sentence forward.

STEP 5. Write the sentence. The one that sounds the best is the sentence to write. This is how all persuasive writing should begin — with a clear, confident opinion statement that the rest of the writing will prove.

(NOTE: Stop there. The first sentence only names the opinion. No details. No "because." See SKILL #5 for where the "because" fits in persuasive writing.)

STEP 2B (Show the children — 5 minutes):
Let me show you how I do this.

Step 1: Name the strongest side. I look back at my T-Chart. (Point to the T-Chart.) I circled Drive thru — that's the side with the most details, the most proof. That's my strongest side. That's what my opinion sentence will be about.

STEP 2. Name the bigger topic. The full prompt that started all this was: "Which is better when ordering and eating food from a restaurant: drive thru or going inside?" I need to choose 1-3 words to include in the opening sentence. Well I definitely can't just say "drive thru." That's totally out of the blue. I need to reference "ordering & eating food."

STEP 3. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. Now I need to pick some opinion words. Let's try: clearly, definitely, & no doubt. I'll test these all to see which one sounds the best.

STEP 4. Put the 3 parts together. Now I put the 3 pieces of information together — 1 of the opinion phrases plus the strongest side ("drive thru") plus "ordering & eating food." I'll start with "clearly."
• "When ordering and eating food from a restaurant, the drive-thru is clearly the better choice." (Pause.) I like "clearly" — it sounds confident and authoritative. I also worked in "better" as a second opinion word. Let me try "definitely."
• "The drive-thru is definitely the way to order & eat food from a restaurant." (Pause.) I like the power of "definitely" but without mentioning the other side, it sounds awkward to be so positive about something. Let me try "no doubt" in a third attempt.
• "There is no doubt that ordering & eating from the drive-thru is better than eating inside." (Pause.) Oooh, I like that. It's a little long, but it sets up the context for my reader. I think it's the best option.

STEP 5. Write the sentence. (Write it slowly while narrating.)

Today, we are learning how to write the opening opinion statement — the first sentence of any persuasive piece. Strong persuasive writing begins with a clear, confident opinion statement that the rest of the writing will prove.

STEP 3 (Interact — We do; I do again, you help me):
Help me with another one.
1. Determine the strongest side. Yesterday, we determined that the best treat was a Candy bar over ice cream.

2. Name the bigger topic. What 3 words from that full prompt do you think should be included? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard several of you mention "best treat."

3. Choose 3 opinion words/phrases. Look at the list of opinion words. Identify 3 you would like to play around with. Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard several possibilities. Let's go with "only, clearly, & should."

4. Put the 3 parts together. Let's start with "only." Put that with "candy bar" and "treat" or "best treat." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say…
• "I think a candy bar is clearly the best treat." What is strong and not-so-strong in this opinion statement? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you note that we don't want to start with "I think…" anymore. That worked in first grade, but not in fourth! OK, let's try an opinion sentence with "clearly." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say…
• "A candy bar is clearly the only treat you should ever pick." Well it's definitely better than the first one. How do you feel about "clearly?" How would the reader take that? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. Let's try a third option using "should." Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me. I heard many of you say…
• "Everyone should choose a candy bar because it is the best treat." Do you like this one better than the second one — why? Turn & Talk. (Eavesdrop 6-10 seconds.) Back to me.

Today, we are learning how to use opinion words and our strongest side from the T-Chart to write the first sentence of our persuasive piece.

STEP 4 (Close — You do; I help):
During Independent Writing Time, you will get out your T-Chart on what is better — Winter break or Summer break? I want you to follow the same process that I just taught you: 1. Name the strongest side. 2. Name the bigger topic. 3. Choose 3 opinion words. 4. Put the parts together. 5. I want you to write 3 opinion sentences — each one using a different opinion word with the strongest side. Now it's your turn!
